Mortgage rates dropped today, but anything above 7% still puts pressure on home buyers’ budgets.

Industry observers note that the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.24% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points lower than yesterday and three basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.).

According to recent reports, A significant drop is eye-catching, but you should consider mortgage interest rates' overall direction, not just what's going on today. While the economy never sleeps, markets are closed on the weekends. The rates you see Friday are unlikely to change much (if at all) until Monday.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:.

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to newly introduced inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

It has been revealed that next week, the Nerds are waiting for the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, due out Wednesday. It's the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation, so investors will be watching closely. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but lenders anticipate its decisions, so mortgage rates often move before the Fed acts. Stubbornly high inflation is a major reason why we’re seeing upward pressure on mortgage rates right now.

If PCE shows inflation comes in hotter than expected, mortgage rates could climb as markets anticipate further Fed rate hikes. (An increase to the federal funds rate is already widely expected at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting.) A cooler reading could ease some pressure on mortgage rates for now.

I’m not getting my hopes up too high for meaningfully lower inflation, though. Last week's Producer Price Index revealed wholesale inflation climbed 6.5% over the past year — its fastest pace in four years. Wholesale inflation measures the price businesses pay for things. When businesses’ costs go up, they could pass those along to consumers in the form of higher prices — keeping the flames of inflation alive.

Whether Wednesday's PCE brings relief or another helping of bad inflation news, we'll know before the turkey hits the table on Thursday.

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you initiative to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.74% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

In a recent development, » Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders.

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

Recent findings suggest that if the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a fresh home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

    #16232. Systems Of Record, Systems Of Action And The Parts Of The Enterprise That Still Don't Have A System

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (900 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    Systems Of Record, Systems Of Action And The Parts Of The Enterprise That Still Don't Have A System

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Kunal Chopra is the CEO of Certivo, an AI-powered compliance system of record for global manufacturers.
    • ​I’ve spent most of my career building enterprise software, and the pattern I keep returning to is simple: A business function matures when it gets a system.
    • Recent findings suggest that A system brings that knowledge into one place everyone can rely on.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Kunal Chopra is the CEO of Certivo, an AI-powered compliance system of record for global manufacturers.

    ​I’ve spent most of my career building enterprise software, and the pattern I keep returning to is simple: A business function matures when it gets a system. Before that, it runs on people, spreadsheets and inboxes. After that, it can be measured, scaled and audited. AI is now changing what a system can do, which makes it worth asking which functions still don’t have one.

    Recent findings suggest that A system brings that knowledge into one place everyone can rely on. It defines what data counts, who owns it and what happens next, so a manufacturer can run the same process a thousand times without depending on the one person who remembers how it’s done. Few systems fully achieve a single source of truth, but the ones that come closest become the foundation the rest of the business is built on.

    Geoffrey Moore popularized the term “systems of record” in a 2011 white paper for AIIM, describing the transactional systems companies had relied on for decades. A system of record is the authoritative source of truth for a domain. Other teams trust it because it agrees with itself.​.

    CRM holds customers, contacts and opportunities, while ERP holds orders, inventory and financials. SCM manages suppliers, purchase orders and logistics, and PLM tracks parts, bills of materials and engineering changes. Each one made its function legible to the rest of the organization, which is why a CFO can close the books and a sales leader can forecast with confidence.

    It has been revealed that systems of record store state, and people have done the work around them: reading documents, reconciling records, deciding what to do and entering the result. AI is moving that work into the system itself. A system of action uses the system of record as its foundation, reads incoming information, interprets it against rules and context and takes the next step: updating the record, requesting a missing document or routing an exception to the right person. Customer support teams already use agents that resolve routine tickets end to end, and finance teams use them for invoice matching and reconciliation.​.

    Industry observers note that the system of record becomes more valuable in this model, because every action depends on the quality of the data and rules underneath it. Leaders evaluating a system of action should ask which actions it takes on its own and which go to a person for approval, how each action traces back to its source and logic and how it handles cases where its confidence is low. In regulated work, those answers need to be reproducible and auditable.

    In a recent development, ​Compliance is the clearest example I know. A manufacturer has to show that its products meet requirements such as REACH, RoHS and PFAS reporting rules. The evidence for that lives everywhere. Supplier declarations arrive as email attachments. Safety data sheets sit in shared drives. A question about a substance gets answered in a Teams thread, and a supplier’s change notice reveals up in Slack. Part data lives in PLM, supplier records in ERP and SCM and customer requests in CRM.​.

    Recent findings suggest that when a customer asks whether a product contains a restricted substance, someone pulls the answer together by hand from all of those places. PwC’s 2025 Global Compliance Survey found that 85% of respondents say compliance requirements have grown more complex over the past three years, so that manual assembly is getting harder every year.​.

    Compliance went without a system for three reasons. It cuts across every other function, so no single system was a natural home. Teams treated it as a periodic project, which made spreadsheets seem good enough. Its data was also too unstructured for traditional software to handle. In an earlier article, I wrote about how AI-native software can work with data in whatever format it arrives. That removes the third barrier, and it means compliance can build its system of record and its system of action at the same time.

    In a recent development, compliance isn’t the only function in this position. Ashu Garg of Foundation Capital has argued that systems of record capture outcomes but not the reasoning behind them. A VP approves a discount in a Slack message, and the CRM records the final price without the approval or the rationale. The same is true of a waiver for a nonconforming part, an extension on supplier payment terms or an exception granted to a key customer.​.

    According to recent reports, those decisions shape how a manufacturer operates, and the precedent they set is often more valuable than the transaction itself. Today that context lives in chat threads, meeting notes and people’s memories. As AI agents take on more work, the absence of a record of why decisions were made becomes a practical constraint, because an agent can’t follow a precedent it can’t see.

    The functions that lack a system tend to share three traits: the work crosses departments, the data lives in conversations and documents and the process depends on judgment. Those were the conditions that kept traditional software out. AI is making them workable.​.

    Where else in your enterprise is crucial work still happening without a system?​.

    According to recent reports, intuit did give investors GAAP guidance on what to expect for the rest of its fiscal 2027, but the news wasn't quite as good. Revenue is forecast between $23.1 billion and $23.4 billion -- no more than 9% growth, again led by Global Business Solutions. Earnings per share are expected to grow less swiftly than in Q1 -- but still pretty quick, rising about 23% to $20.24 per share.

    Assuming Intuit hits that mark, at its current $284 share price, the stock would be trading at only 14 times current-year earnings -- quite cheap for a 23% grower.

    The bad news is that most analysts doubt Intuit can keep growing at this rate long-term. Average analyst forecasts are closer to 13.5% growth. Between the growth rate and the 1.8% dividend yield, though, I still see Intuit stock as at worst fairly priced -- and probably a bit of a bargain.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Maria Zhang is the CEO and Co-Founder of Palona.

    Physical AI must understand the operation and keep that understanding accurate as conditions change.​.

    A physical AI demo can make a difficult problem look solved. But it establishes what the system can do under the conditions shown. A business needs that capability to hold as workloads, layouts and routines change.

    The gap between AI adoption and business value is familiar. McKinsey’s 2026 survey (login required) found nearly nine in 10 respondents reported AI use in at least one business function within their organizations. Only about 6% reported both significant impact and at least 5% of earnings before interest and taxes attributable to AI.

    Industry observers note that in my previous article, I explored a coding agent for physical businesses. Delivering that promise requires a reliable, continuously updated understanding of the operation.

    In many knowledge-intensive applications, a foundation model needs specialized knowledge: a law firm’s precedents, internal policies or proprietary history.

    Much of that context already exists in documents or structured records. Retrieval supplies relevant material, fine-tuning adapts models to specialized tasks and workflow integration connects them to the business.

    According to recent reports, physical businesses need these capabilities, too. They also contain important information that has never been recorded.

    Recent findings suggest that an order system may record when work began and ended without showing where an employee waited or which handoff stalled. A language model cannot retrieve events the system never captured.

    According to recent reports, physical AI must observe that activity and interpret its business meaning, drawing on knowledge of the operation. This is part of perception.

    Sources indicate that consider measuring how promptly a restaurant line moves. Detecting people does not distinguish someone waiting to order from someone collecting food or waiting for a friend.

    An experienced operator reads relationships and context. The AI must understand what people are doing, how interactions change and when the evidence is incomplete.

    A staffing recommendation can be logically consistent with the reported queue while responding to a queue that does not exist. Strong reasoning can still produce the wrong decision from a mistaken account of the operation.​.

    Vision-language-action models, or VLAs, connect visual observations and language instructions to actions. World models learn how environments evolve to support prediction and planning. Simulation and digital twins provide virtual environments for training and testing; their usefulness depends on fidelity to relevant conditions.

    These capabilities can support different architectures. An end-to-end system that observes, plans and acts may be appropriate for some applications.

    A modular approach connects foundation models, domain knowledge, business rules and workflow systems through explicit interfaces.

    I believe a useful boundary is the translation from physical observations into meaningful operational states.

    Industry observers note that the system might estimate that a customer is waiting, an order is ready or a task is blocked. Recorded events, such as an observed handoff, help track state changes.

    For business decisions, this is more useful than object detections or generic captions.

    Much of the business problem can then be expressed symbolically: as people, objects, events, relationships and rules. Language models, planners and workflow systems can use these representations to evaluate alternatives and coordinate action.

    Recent findings suggest that the representation must preserve timing, evidence and uncertainty. A robot may still require detailed geometry; an order-status decision can often use a more abstract description.

    According to recent reports, this boundary makes the system more modular. Changing an acceptable wait-time threshold need not require retraining the model that recognizes when service begins. It also helps teams distinguish observation or interpretation errors from failures in reasoning, planning or execution.

    For operators, “The order is ready, but no handoff has been observed” is something they can check. If the handoff area was out of view, missing evidence cannot establish that no handoff occurred.

    The goal is meaningful points of inspection, without requiring every internal neural representation to be explainable.

    Camera placement, resolution and viewing angle affect what can be observed. Lighting, obstructions, connectivity and packaging changes affect whether the complete system keeps working. A strong model cannot reliably recover information its installation never captures. Even when the information is available, conditions that differ from training and testing can expose weaknesses.

    Industry observers note that starbucks’s inventory-counting rollout illustrates the challenge. In September 2025, NomadGo declared deployment to more than 11,000 North American locations, advertising 99% accuracy.

    In a recent development, fast Company reported refrigerator reflections doubling milk counts, Wi-Fi failures erasing scan progress and packaging changes that could require weeks of adaptation. Reuters reported that Starbucks retired the tool in May 2026, citing standardization and consistency.

    Reliable operation depends on the model, its inputs, software and workflow together.

    A model can work, and the deployment can still fail.

    Reliability requires good models, systems engineering and sustained work with customers. Operators reveal exceptions and environmental changes that should inform model development, evaluation and installation practices.

    According to recent reports, this is why we are developing Interaction Tracking as a primary modeling objective. Many meaningful changes in an operation are expressed through interactions among people and objects, within particular spaces and workflows. Tracking those interactions can estimate the business states that downstream reasoning needs.​.

    For buyers, the important questions extend beyond what the demo can do: What does the system actually understand, how can that understanding be checked and how will the vendor keep it reliable as conditions change? For investors, the manufacturer’s technical advantage deserves examination at the level of the complete deployed system.

    According to recent reports, A system can reason convincingly about the wrong situation and execute the wrong action precisely. Closing physical AI’s deployment gap means maintaining a reliable understanding of the operation as it changes.​.

    Inside: what the hawkish Fed minutes mean for client conversations, equal-weight versus cap-weight S&P 500 funds after the Nvidia wobble, why Nvidia's strong quarter and higher outlook didn’t lift the stock, the IRS's 2027 retirement-proposal limits, and a Thanksgiving-week calendar worth bookmarking.

    Recent findings suggest that last week's inflation report raised the question; this week's FOMC minutes mostly answered it. The Fed is no longer asking whether to keep turning the thermostat down (it is raising rates), only how many degrees at a time. Here is the short version for the call.

    The honest caveat: Not everyone expects a long campaign. Nuveen's fixed-income team, for one, still looks for just one more hike this year followed by an extended hold through 2027, and says markets are pricing a steeper path than that. Translation: the direction is clear, the destination is not, so initiative for a range.

    Putting it to work with clients:.

    Recent findings suggest that client-ready line: "The Fed is still raising rates because the economy is holding up and prices are stubborn. We can't predict how far it goes, so we're planning for a range, not a forecast.".

    What it means for your practice:.

    Sources indicate that tech's slide has put losses on the books in some taxable accounts, and there are six weeks left to use them. Realized losses offset realized gains dollar for dollar, then up to $3,000 of ordinary income, with the rest carried forward. The catch is the wash-sale rule: buying the same or a substantially identical security within 30 days before or after the sale disallows the loss, and that includes purchases in a spouse's account or an IRA. Pair this with last week's year-end distribution estimates, since a harvested loss can absorb a fund's capital gain payout. Try: "The recent drop gives us a chance to turn paper losses into a lower tax bill, and I'll make sure the replacement holding keeps you invested.".

    Nvidia answered last week's question and walked straight into a fresh one. In its first report since Jensen Huang's resignation, the company beat on revenue, earnings and guidance, then watched its shares jump after hours and flip to a loss. The stock closed down about 3.3% Thursday and is down more than a quarter this month, about $2.2 trillion below its October peak in market value.

    Recent findings suggest that our read: the numbers back up last week's argument that the business is intact. Kress also remarked Nvidia's additional share repurchases now top $150 billion, and told CNBC the board has no plans to bring Huang back. But the stock was never trading on this quarter. It is trading on three open questions: who runs Nvidia permanently, how much margin gives way as volume climbs, and how long customers keep spending on AI at this pace. One analyst told Reuters the quarter was the kind Nvidia has delivered for years, which is exactly the point: a beat is the price of admission, not a catalyst. What to do with Nvidia shares still depends on position size and why a client owns them: a large position bought on conviction in one leader deserves a risk check, while a smaller position held for the products and AI demand has a thesis that this quarter supported.

    With a Fed hike all but priced in, tech still swinging, and the holidays here, this is a good week to reach out before clients wonder whether they should call you. Here is an email or call opener:.

    It has been revealed that prioritize clients nearing retirement, clients with concentrated tech or employer-stock positions, and clients with variable-rate debt ahead of the Dec. 9 meeting.

    Clients will ask, and some will have been tempted to chase it. A few points worth having ready:.

    The most a 401(k) participant aged 60 to 63 can defer in 2027: the latest $25,500 limit plus the $11,750 SECURE 2.0 “super” catch-up.

    It has been revealed that why it matters to advisors: Clients in the final stretch before retirement can use this window to catch up swiftly, and many don't know it exists. Try: "Between ages 60 and 63, you can save more in your 401(k) than at any other point in your career. Let's see what that would do for your retirement date.".

    Is Altria's 5.6% Dividend Yield Too Good to Be True Heading Into 2027?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (933 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that one of the great dividends of our age is paid by a tech giant making products so unfashionable they're barely visible anymore.
    • Recent findings suggest that several decades ago, it was rare to visit a household, office, or restaurant where at least one occupant wasn't lighting up.
    • According to recent reports, given the many restrictions on traditional tobacco consumption in the U.S., plus the increasing health consciousness of its population, it's a wonder Altria ekes out any growth at all.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Eric Volkman – Nov 20, 2026 at 12:56PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Altria Group ›.

    Sources indicate that one of the great dividends of our age is paid by a tech giant making products so unfashionable they're barely visible anymore. I'm talking about Altria (MO +0.68%), the latest iteration of a storied tobacco enterprise that created and still sells the iconic Marlboro brand in this country.

    Recent findings suggest that several decades ago, it was rare to visit a household, office, or restaurant where at least one occupant wasn't lighting up. These days, it's normal to go days, weeks, even months without encountering any smokers. The cigarettes that remain the hard core of Altria's production to this day aren't a growing market. So it's worthwhile to explore whether the company's famously high-yield dividend -- which at the moment pays out at 5.6% -- is sustainable for much longer. Here's my take on that.

    According to recent reports, given the many restrictions on traditional tobacco consumption in the U.S., plus the increasing health consciousness of its population, it's a wonder Altria ekes out any growth at all. In the company's third quarter, its net revenue only crept up by 1% year over year to $6.13 billion. If we strip excise (or "sin") taxes out of the equation, we get a meatier growth figure of 3.6%, with revenue net of such obligations of $5.44 billion. But that improvement was largely due to price increases, as total shipment volume of smokeables sank by 2.9%.

    Revenue net of excise taxes, by the way, is considered the yardstick top-line figure for tobacco companies, so I'll stay with that throughout this piece without repeating the descriptor.

    Sources indicate that of that $5.44 billion, smokeable products -- anchored by Marlboro -- pulled in $4.76 billion, or 88% of the total. Almost all of the remainder ($667 million) consisted of oral tobacco products, the revenue for which rose only marginally during the period. There's one bright spot there, however, and that's the company's promising on! and on! PLUS nicotine pouches, which collectively experienced a 13% increase in shipment volume.

    Years ago, Altria sensibly tried to pivot toward products with a brighter future, specifically next-generation tobacco offerings seen as more innovative and (relatively) healthier. But its attempts to develop a vape in-house flopped, as did its acquisitions of stakes in existing vape manufacturers (most notably the spectacular flameout of the once-promising Juul Labs). These days, the manufacturer's "all other" category covers the tiny sales of such goods, which amounted to $12 million in the quarter.

    NYSE · As of 2:17 PM ET 11/20/26.

    Non-GAAP (adjusted) profitability, like revenue, didn't bounce sharply higher for Altria. It improved by 4% to $2.55 billion in the quarter. This, however, makes for a sky-high net margin of 47%. Most companies would be satisfied with a percentage in the low double digits. What's the secret sauce with Altria?

    In a recent development, it's about the core product. Cigarettes are addictive, so users not only come back time and again to buy them, but they're also willing to put up with the frequent price raises by makers like Altria (and to fork over the always-high excise taxes to boot). Given that, there's little or no reason for a manufacturer to innovate the product, and to top it all off, cigarettes are cheap to make.

    Put all of this together, and you have a good that generates high profits at very modest and steady costs. That's why, even in this day and age, tobacco companies continue to be cash-generating machines. Altria's statement of cash flows is always a thing of beauty, with high operating flows and tiny investments resulting in a mighty gush of free cash flow (FCF). This was only slightly down year over year in the third quarter, to almost $3 billion. That's far more than the under $1.8 billion the company needed to fund that high-yield dividend, plus stock-boosting share repurchases totaling $400 million.

    American smokers aren't going to change their habits much, so Altria felt confident enough to raise its full-year 2026 earnings guidance. Adjusted net income should rise by 4.5% to 6% over the 2025 figure to $5.66 to $5.74 per share, the tech giant believes. All that cash flow has to go somewhere, so the company's board authorized a $1 billion expansion of its existing share repurchase program, which had $265 million remaining. The initiative has also been extended, with the upcoming deadline being Dec. 31, 2027.

    Industry observers note that both of these moves strongly indicate Altria will keep its now 57-year (!) dividend raise streak alive, maintaining its status as a Dividend King (one of the few stocks that have raised their payout for at least 50 consecutive years). After all, its payout is one of the stock's great draws, and management is acutely aware of its importance. I predict, with the same level of confidence as Altria's leaders revealed the guidance raise and the share buyback news, that it'll continue to deliver those high-margin profits and impressive levels of FCF.

    And with that, this perpetually high-yield dividend is extremely safe, in my opinion.

    #16218. How Often Do You Need To Scrub The Do Not Call List? The 31-Day Rule Explained

    How Often Do You Need To Scrub The Do Not Call List? The 31-Day Rule Explained

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Phil Portman is a serial entrepreneur and the Founder & CEO of Textdrip — a small business SMS marketing tool to automate SMS campaigns.
    • According to recent reports, ​I see businesses repeatedly making the same mistake: They scrub their contact list once and then keep calling and texting from that list for months.
    • Industry observers note that after years of experience working in a regulated industry, I’m sure about one thing: Businesses rarely fail because the rules are unclear.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Phil Portman is a serial entrepreneur and the Founder & CEO of Textdrip — a small business SMS marketing tool to automate SMS campaigns.

    According to recent reports, ​I see businesses repeatedly making the same mistake: They scrub their contact list once and then keep calling and texting from that list for months. That’s a risky habit, because every day newly introduced numbers join the Do Not Call Registry. A list that was clean in January can be full of problems by March.

    Industry observers note that after years of experience working in a regulated industry, I’m sure about one thing: Businesses rarely fail because the rules are unclear. They fail because their processes break down in practice. The Do Not Call rules are a crystal-clear example of this.

    In a recent development, how often do you have to scrub the Do Not Call (DNC) list? Every 31 days. To keep safe harbor protection, you need to scrub against a version of the registry that is no more than 31 days old. In practice, that means every month.

    The National Do Not Call Registry is run by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC). It lets people add their personal phone numbers to a list that tells telemarketers to stop contacting them. It exists to protect consumers who don’t want sales calls. It covers personal numbers, such as home and mobile lines. It doesn’t cover business-to-business calls to a company line. Knowing this difference helps you decide which numbers need a check.

    Many teams assume it only covers voice calls, but it doesn’t. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) treats text messages as calls, so the same protections apply to SMS marketing. If you text prospects, those numbers also need a DNC check.

    State lists exist as well. Some states keep their own Do Not Call lists, and some, such as Florida and Texas, have stricter rules than the federal registry. If you contact people in several states, you need to check each state’s rules before you launch.

    According to recent reports, some calls are exempt, such as those to people who gave written permission or have an established business relationship with you. Even then, you must honor opt-out requests.

    To qualify for safe harbor under FTC and FCC regulations, telemarketers must scrub their list against the National DNC Registry. Every call must be made using a registry version downloaded no more than 31 days earlier. Simply put, you must rescrub every month. If it’s day 32, you’re already at risk.

    According to recent reports, suppose you scrubbed a list on the first of the month. On the 20th, a prospect joins the registry. Your team keeps working that same list. Any call made after day 31 relies on an outdated version. Many teams scrub only when they upload fresh leads. This sounds fine, but a campaign can run for weeks, and a number can join the registry halfway through. If you keep contacting that number, you’re working from outdated data.

    Safe harbor is a defense that protects a business when a call goes out by mistake. But it only applies if you had a working process in place before the mistake happened. A written policy that nobody reads or follows won’t help. Training without a current list won’t help either.

    The FCC rule lists what a DNC safe harbor process needs:.

    • Written Do Not Call procedures.

    • Staff trained on those procedures.

    • An internal Do Not Call list that is kept up to date.

    • Registry access used to scrub within the 31-day window.

    • Logs (records) showing when each scrub happened.

    Record-keeping is a common gap. Without records, you have no safe harbor, even if the scrub did happen. If a regulator or a lawyer asks for proof, saying “we did it” won’t be enough. You need proof (dates and logs).

    Do Not Call violations get expensive rapidly. Under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act (TCPA), a consumer can sue for $500 per violation. If the violation was willful or knowing, a court can raise that to $1,500 per violation. A consumer generally must receive more than one call from the same business within 12 months to bring a DNC claim.

    According to recent reports, some of these claims are filed as class actions. One outdated list can hold thousands of people, and each one may have a claim. A small gap in your process can turn into a very large bill. Legal fees and settlements add to that, along with damage to your business reputation.

    I lead a tech giant in a regulated industry, so I think about this often. Compliance works best when it is practiced as a routine instead of an event. We built Landline Remover to help teams make scrubbing a routine.

    1. Scrub every time you upload leads, not just on launch day.

    2. Rescrub active lists monthly, ideally a few days before the 31-day window closes.

    Industry observers note that 3. Check your internal list and the national list together. Your internal do-not-call list holds people who told you directly to stop. The registry doesn’t know about them. Both lists matter.

    Industry observers note that 4. Check reassigned numbers. Numbers change owners. The FCC’s reassigned numbers database can tell you whether a number has changed hands since you got consent.

    5. Log every scrub with the date. That log is your proof if a court or regulator asks.

    In a recent development, 6. Automate the scrubbing process so it doesn’t depend on memory.

    Do Not Call compliance is a monthly habit, not a one-time task. The rule is simple: scrub within 31 days, every time.

    DNC scrubbing alone can’t protect a business. You need to keep proof that you followed the rule. Scrubbing only protects you if you can prove it. So build a regular scrubbing habit and keep the records. Remember that regulators don’t just look at your efforts—they ask for evidence.

    #16215. Breaking: Your Employees’ Personal AI Agents Are Becoming Your Security Problem

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1021 w)

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Your Employees’ Personal AI Agents Are Becoming Your Security Problem

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1021 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • David Goldschlag is co-founder and CEO of Aembit, an identity control plane for AI agents.
    • ​Ahead of an important client meeting, a sales representative connects their personal AI agent to manufacturer email and files.
    • Industry observers note that personal AI agents, including Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots and Google’s Gemini Spark, are software assistants that can carry out routine tasks across connected services and continue working between conversations.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    David Goldschlag is co-founder and CEO of Aembit, an identity control plane for AI agents.

    ​Ahead of an important client meeting, a sales representative connects their personal AI agent to manufacturer email and files. The setup takes minutes and allows the employee to arrive prepared with considerably less effort, but that well-meaning shortcut may carry risks the rep never considered.

    Industry observers note that personal AI agents, including Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots and Google’s Gemini Spark, are software assistants that can carry out routine tasks across connected services and continue working between conversations. It is early, and there is little data yet on how often employees connect these personal assistants to organization accounts. But if the first numbers are any indication, the habit is forming swiftly. Meta noted Muse passed 10 million accounts within roughly six weeks of launch, and a Menlo Ventures survey found that 32% of U.S. adults who use AI have already let it act on their behalf without final sign-off.

    Sources indicate that for security leaders who remember the first requests to connect personal smartphones to company email, the arrival of these agentic deputies has a familiar feel. Employees found something useful and expected to use it, while IT and security were left to reconcile that enthusiasm with responsibility for company data.

    Bring-your-own-device (BYOD) policies and years of “shadow IT” disputes established an enduring reality: The rank and file would have a say in the technology they used. But the analogy has limits in the AI era. Traditional software generally follows predefined workflows, while an agent can choose which tools to use and which steps to take in carrying out an employee’s request, without the employee directing each action.

    Permissions granted with little consideration during setup can later support a series of actions the employee never specifically contemplated. For CISOs, the difficulty is deciding how much authority should accompany that discretion and how to enforce those limits once an AI assistant begins working.

    Consider the employee preparing for the customer meeting. The request of their agent sounds innocuous: Review recent correspondence, find the relevant account documents and prepare a briefing.

    Yet the permissions available during setup may cover far more information than this assignment requires. Depending on the connection, the agent may receive access to a mailbox containing correspondence with hundreds of customers, along with internal discussions unrelated to the meeting.

    Suppose the employee also asks the agent to prepare and send an external follow-up. An internal document contains useful background, including an unannounced pricing change. The agent could incorporate that information into a customer message because it appears relevant to the assignment. Every connection involved might be permitted, even though the resulting disclosure was never intended. Read-only access offers limited reassurance if the agent can send what it reads through another service.

    Requiring employee approval before an agent receives access provides another safeguard, but its value depends on what the employee can reasonably assess. A consent screen can describe the permissions being requested without making clear how an agent could use them together. The employee may approve those permissions without anticipating the disclosure described above.

    Recent findings suggest that company policy must establish which resources an assistant may access and which actions require further review. Employees should understand their responsibilities, but connecting an agent should not leave them to determine how much authority the company is willing to delegate.

    The following practices can help security leaders establish those boundaries while giving employees a practical way to use personal AI agents.

    Verify that records identify which agent acted and whose authority it used. Logs that name only the employee may leave investigators unable to distinguish direct actions from those taken by an agent.

    In a recent development, establish which accounts and resources it can access, whether it can act in the background and how the provider handles credentials and retrieved data. Approval of an assistant should not imply approval of every connection it supports.

    Where controls permit, restrict access to relevant resources and separate retrieval permissions from permission to publish or send. Enforce those limits at runtime, when the agent requests access. If a service offers only broad access, weigh that limitation in the approval decision.

    Reserve employees’ attention for consequential decisions. Before an external message is sent, for example, let them review its recipients, attachments and exact content, with another review required if material details change.

    Industry observers note that ensure security can revoke an agent’s access without disabling the employee’s account. This gives security teams a way to intervene when an agent needs to be stopped. Here, that means access revocation: withdrawing the agent’s ability to use connected systems. Cutting off access, however, does not necessarily terminate the agent’s process.

    Test it against background activity and previously issued credentials, and measure how long it takes for subsequent requests to fail. Depending on the implementation, previously issued access tokens may remain usable until they expire, or a revocation decision may take time to reach every system involved. Incident procedures should account for the behavior observed in testing, including any additional steps required to contain ongoing activity.​​​.

    According to recent reports, these practices also expose limitations that a policy document alone cannot resolve. If a provider cannot support sufficiently narrow access or useful audit records, the tech giant may need to restrict the information available to that agent or decline the connection.​.

    In a recent development, the BYOD experience offers a useful lesson about AI adoption. Employees’ preferences can influence tech giant technology decisions long before a formal policy catches up. Security leaders should take seriously the reasons people want personal agents, including the convenience of using a tool they already know.

    In a recent development, A workable policy should give employees a clear route to request access, explain which uses are permitted and offer alternatives when a requested connection grants more authority than the business can accept. Security teams, in turn, need evidence that the agreed restrictions hold during actual use.​​​.

    Industry News: The Next Software Revolution After AI Is Efficiency

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Itamar Syn-Hershko, Founder of NeverBlink AI and BigData Boutique, helps companies confidently operate and optimize data platforms at scale.
    • For decades, we’ve made software easier to write, even when it meant making it more expensive to run.​.
    • In a recent development, we introduced programming languages, frameworks and layers of abstraction that allowed developers to move faster.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Itamar Syn-Hershko, Founder of NeverBlink AI and BigData Boutique, helps companies confidently operate and optimize data platforms at scale.

    For decades, we’ve made software easier to write, even when it meant making it more expensive to run.​.

    In a recent development, we introduced programming languages, frameworks and layers of abstraction that allowed developers to move faster. Along the way, we accepted higher memory consumption, more CPU usage and increasingly complex infrastructure.​.

    Industry observers note that for the most part, this made sense. Developers were expensive, hardware kept getting cheaper and getting products to market quickly was often more vital than squeezing the most out of every server.​.

    I think we’re approaching a point where that trade-off no longer makes sense.​.

    According to recent reports, AI is changing the cost of writing software, while the growing demand for computing resources is making efficiency more important than it has been in years. Together, these forces could change not just how we build software but also the economics of the entire software industry.​.

    It has been revealed that take Java, for example. Much of its success came from making developers more productive. Automatic memory management, a rich ecosystem and portability made it easier to build and maintain complex applications without worrying about many of the details involved in lower-level programming.​.

    Industry observers note that the trade-off was additional runtime overhead. Garbage collection, managed memory and abstraction layers can require considerably more resources than a carefully optimized native implementation.​.

    Sources indicate that this was often a perfectly reasonable compromise. If using Java saved months of engineering work, spending a little more on servers was easy to justify.​.

    But what happens when AI can write, maintain and optimize complex C++ or Rust code at a fraction of the previous engineering cost?​ We should start questioning whether some of the abstractions we’ve relied on for decades are still worth their price.​.

    Recent findings suggest that I’m not suggesting we rewrite every Java application in assembly. There are good reasons to use managed languages, including their mature tooling, ecosystems and safety characteristics. AI-generated code also introduces its own risks and still needs careful review.​.

    But the argument that lower-level programming is too expensive or complicated to justify is becoming much weaker.​.

    ​At the same time, the infrastructure side of the equation is changing.​.

    AI is creating enormous demand for computing capacity, memory, electricity and data center space. The International Energy Agency projects that global data center electricity consumption will roughly double by 2030.​.

    According to recent reports, we cannot keep solving every software performance problem by adding more hardware. At some point, the availability and cost of that hardware become serious constraints.​.

    There’s also growing pressure to make software cheaper.​.

    Recent findings suggest that AI is already reducing the time and effort involved in producing software, and we should expect some of those savings to reach customers. As it becomes cheaper to build competing products, companies will find it harder to justify high prices based on development costs alone.​.

    According to recent reports, this puts infrastructure efficiency at the center of the conversation. If two products offer comparable functionality but one requires a fraction of the hardware to operate, the difference can be substantial. The more efficient product can offer lower prices, better margins or both.​.

    ​Search engines and databases are good places to look for early examples.

    Sources indicate that ​Traditional search architectures (Lucene-based especially, such as Elasticsearch and OpenSearch) often require continuously provisioned compute resources and substantial memory to maintain indexes and deliver low-latency queries. This can make infrastructure costs difficult to align with fluctuating workloads.​.

    It has been revealed that ​Companies such as turbopuffer and WarpSearch are challenging those assumptions. Both use an object-storage-first architecture for vector and full-text search, reducing the need to keep large indexes on expensive infrastructure. A Google Cloud case study reports search and storage cost reductions of 90% for its approach.

    ​There are examples outside search as well, including ClickHouse, Neon, Bun and more.

    ​These products aren’t necessarily the result of AI-assisted development. Many of their innovations started before today’s coding agents became widely available.

    ​What interests me is what happens when the engineering effort required to build systems like these drops dramatically.

    ​For engineering leaders, this should change how we evaluate technology choices.

    ​We spend a lot of time measuring developer productivity, feature delivery and time to market. We should be paying just as much attention to what our software costs to operate.

    Industry observers note that ​That starts with measuring actual resource consumption. Cost per query, cost per transaction, memory per workload and CPU utilization are not just infrastructure metrics. They directly affect the economics of the product.

    ​It also means questioning architectural decisions we’ve come to accept. Does that service really need to run continuously? Does that dataset need to stay in memory? Are we using the right algorithms and data structures? Could a more efficient implementation eliminate entire servers?

    ​And perhaps most importantly, we should be using AI for more than producing code faster.

    ​AI can help investigate performance bottlenecks, evaluate alternative algorithms, rewrite expensive components and explore lower-level implementations that would previously have required too much engineering effort.

    In a recent development, ​There are still trade-offs. Reliability, security, correctness and maintainability matter. An implementation that saves 20% in CPU costs but introduces serious operational risks is hardly an improvement.

    ​The point is that we now have more ways to pursue efficiency without paying the same development cost we once did.

    ​I expect we’ll see more companies challenge established software categories by building products that achieve similar results with much less infrastructure.

    ​Some will use better algorithms. Others will rethink storage architectures, eliminate unnecessary compute or replace expensive runtime components. AI will make many of these approaches easier to implement.

    Industry observers note that ​For established software vendors, this creates a real challenge. Their existing architectures may have been designed around assumptions that no longer hold, while newer competitors have the freedom to start from scratch.

    ​For customers, it should eventually mean more capable software at lower prices.

    ​We’ve spent decades making software easier and cheaper to write and accepting the infrastructure overhead that came with it.

    ​Now that writing software is becoming cheaper, it’s time to focus on making it cheaper to run.

    The Portland Trail Blazers made the trek to Milwaukee last year to play the Bucks. Damian Lillard was present, even though he was sitting out the entire 2025-26 campaign — his first season back with the Trail Blazers — as he recovered from the Achilles tear he suffered while playing for the Bucks in their 2025 first-round playoff series.

    Fiserv Forum aired a video tribute to Lillard amid that November 2025 meeting, and the nine-time All-Star received a standing ovation after it played that night.

    Thursday marked the 36-year-old guard's first time taking the court against Milwaukee since his injury and his two-season stint with the Bucks. Lillard was subdued talking about the matchup in the lead-up to tip-off, but he came away with his best performance in 624 days.

    March 5, 2025, was the last time Lillard had a 30-point game. He scored a season-high 33 points on Thursday in a 124-114 victory over a reeling and rebuilding Milwaukee (1-15).

    Portland (10-5) bounced back after dropping consecutive games to the Minnesota Timberwolves.

    According to recent reports, lillard once again received a warm welcome from Bucks fans. Milwaukee ultimately waived him to sign center Myles Turner in the summer of 2025. The Bucks are still paying Lillard after they decided to stretch the remaining $113 million on his contract.

    So, on Thursday, Milwaukee fans watched their team lose its 12th straight game and Lillard shoot 10 of 18 from the field, including 5 of 12 from the beyond the arc.

    Recent findings suggest that plus, another former Bucks player, Jrue Holiday — part of Milwaukee's NBA championship team in 2020-21 — put on a show of his own. He logged 22 points, 7 assists and 4 steals.

    Sources indicate that holiday stepped back to hit a crucial jumper with about 5 ½ minutes to go. Another 36-year-old guard, Holiday went on to help the Trail Blazers create separation late, even coupling a steal with a layup.

    Portland also got 27 points and seven rebounds from a much younger member of its backcourt: Scoot Henderson.

    Meanwhile, the Bucks fell again, a day removed from facing Giannis Antetokounmpo for the first time.

    Milwaukee had four players score 15-plus points this time out. Tyler Herro led the way with 19, Kasparas Jakučionis and Nate Ament had 18 apiece and Ryan Rollins chipped in 15. Turner, notably, was out with a shoulder injury.

    The lead changed hands incessantly on Thursday. Herro drew the Bucks within one at the 3:18 mark in the fourth quarter. The Trail Blazers, though, scored the final nine points, with Lillard netting the last two at the free-throw line.

    #16209. What Security Teams Still Get Wrong About Asset Visibility

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1010 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    What Security Teams Still Get Wrong About Asset Visibility

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Yochai Corem is GM of Exposure Management at Check Point Software.
    • Organizations have more asset data than ever, but turning that data into a reliable view of what they own, operate and expose remains difficult.
    • A server appears in three tools with different identifiers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Yochai Corem is GM of Exposure Management at Check Point Software.

    Organizations have more asset data than ever, but turning that data into a reliable view of what they own, operate and expose remains difficult.

    A server appears in three tools with different identifiers. A cloud workload has an owner who has left the business. A forgotten website remains online after the campaign that funded it has ended. Each leaves security teams with information they still have to investigate before they can act.

    Sources indicate that security leaders should judge asset visibility by how reliably it supports a decision. A useful inventory helps teams establish what an asset does, who is responsible for it, how it is protected and what should happen when a problem appears.

    Several familiar assumptions prevent organizations from reaching that standard.

    An incomplete configuration management database (CMDB) should prompt a review of how records are created, updated and retired.

    It has been revealed that start by defining its purpose. The CMDB should record the systems, services and dependencies needed to manage business operations, with accountable owners and lifecycle status. Detailed security telemetry can remain in specialist systems, linked through reliable identifiers. An impersonating website belongs in an external threat register connected to the affected brand.

    Then identify which sources can reveal missing records. Cloud platforms, endpoint management, identity providers, vulnerability scanners and procurement systems can each expose inconsistencies. Buying a service should trigger registration; retiring it should trigger checks that access, infrastructure and records have been removed.

    Reconciliation should reflect the pace of change. I would set a daily reconciliation target for cloud and endpoint feeds; use deployment and retirement events to trigger updates; and review unresolved discrepancies weekly. Quarterly ownership reviews can supplement those checks.

    It has been revealed that an asset without an owner needs an interim accountable team and an escalation deadline. “Unknown” should describe an investigation in progress.

    The modern attack surface spans internal infrastructure, cloud workloads, software as a service (SaaS), internet-facing systems, supplier connections and the organization’s broader digital presence.

    Those categories need different forms of accountability. Infrastructure teams may manage servers, cloud teams manage workloads and business application owners sponsor SaaS services. Marketing or regional teams may control domains and social accounts. Supplier relationships require a business sponsor alongside technical oversight.

    Security should establish a review and response process across those boundaries. A newly discovered domain needs ownership verification and an assessment of what it hosts. An unfamiliar SaaS service needs checks on its owners, data and access. A fraudulent social account needs investigation and a disruption process.

    Review frequency should follow exposure and change, with continuous discovery where practical and scheduled reviews for ownership, supplier access and dormant services. This broader scope aligns with the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) inclusion of hardware, software, services and supplier services in asset management.

    Leaders can test this assumption by following a newly discovered asset through the security process.

    Does discovery trigger checks for required endpoint protection, vulnerability scanning and an accountable owner? Does an unmanaged internet-facing system reach someone authorized to restrict or remove it? Can the organization confirm that the resulting action occurred?

    It has been revealed that these outcomes show whether visibility operates as a security control. The Center for Internet Security’s (CIS) Control 1 connects inventory management with identifying and addressing unauthorized or unmanaged assets.

    Useful measures include the time taken to assign ownership, the proportion of applicable assets covered by required controls and the age of unresolved discrepancies. A growing inventory count provides little reassurance when newly discovered systems remain unmanaged.

    Additional tools introduce additional records, each with its own identifiers, timestamps and assumptions.

    Sources indicate that effective reconciliation requires explicit rules. Stable cloud resource identifiers or device identifiers should take precedence over an Internet Protocol (IP) address that may change or be reused. Records need source and freshness information so teams can distinguish a current observation from a stale entry.

    Organizations also need rules for conflicting fields. The identity system may establish who uses a device, while a service registry identifies the team accountable for the application it supports. Those relationships should remain distinguishable.

    Recent findings suggest that cyber asset attack surface management (CAASM) can support this work. Organizations can also improve CMDB integrations, use cloud asset inventories and service catalogs, or build reconciliation workflows in their existing data platforms. The operational requirements remain consistent: reliable matching, clear authority for each field and a process for resolving exceptions.

    Discovery should initiate a decision about management, protection or retirement.

    A forgotten website needs an owner to confirm whether it still serves a business purpose. A vulnerable application needs assessment of its exposure, dependencies and operational constraints before a response is selected.

    That decision should remain traceable through completion. If a service is retired, verify that it is no longer reachable. If a security control is applied, confirm that it covers the intended asset. Updating the inventory should accompany the operational change.

    This ongoing connection between asset information and action also underpins continuous threat exposure management (CTEM).

    CTEM depends on this discipline throughout scoping, discovery, prioritization, validation and mobilization.

    Industry observers note that an unknown asset cannot enter the prioritization process. A known asset without business context is difficult to rank. Missing dependencies weaken assessments of attack paths and change impact. An unknown owner delays action, while stale records undermine confirmation that an exposure has been reduced.

    CAASM and external attack surface management (EASM) can support these stages by reconciling internal records and discovering internet-facing assets. Their value depends on the ownership, decision rules and response processes surrounding them.

    According to recent reports, security leaders should expect asset visibility to connect discovery with accountable action. Every significant asset needs enough current context for someone to determine its protection requirements, address its exposures and verify the result. That is how a reliable inventory helps reduce the opportunities available to an attacker.​.

    #16203. How To Teach Your AI Agent About Your Company

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (800 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    How To Teach Your AI Agent About Your Company

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (800 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Frederik Riskær Pedersen, Founder and CEO of Maplith, a firm brain for your AI agents.
    • Industry observers note that for 16 years, I ran a translation tech giant that grew from a handful of people into an international business.
    • Industry observers note that one customer indicates it well.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Frederik Riskær Pedersen, Founder and CEO of Maplith, a firm brain for your AI agents.

    Industry observers note that for 16 years, I ran a translation tech giant that grew from a handful of people into an international business. The most vital thing I learned about knowledge is that it rarely lives where you think it does.

    Industry observers note that one customer indicates it well. We had to fetch their files from their own system and deliver them in their own layout, and we could only invoice some of the repetitions. None of that was written down anywhere. It lived with one project manager. Anyone else would have done it the standard way and got it wrong.

    Recent findings suggest that that tailoring was not a side issue. It was the product. If the work had been standard, the customer could have run the model themselves. This is why a tech giant’s rules never get standardized away: The exceptions are often exactly what customers pay for.

    According to recent reports, I think of this every time someone asks me why their AI agent isn’t delivering. The models are good enough. The problem is that the agent starts from zero every time. It does not know which systems you run, how they connect or which rules you follow without ever writing them down. So it guesses, and a confident guess in your accounts is worse than no answer at all.

    Here are five things you can do this month before you let an agent work inside your business. None of them needs a newly introduced tool.

    Book two hours with the three or four people who make most of the everyday decisions. Ask them one question: “What would a upcoming hire ask you in their first week?” The answers are your unwritten rules: which customers get special terms, when a refund is approved, what can be invoiced and what cannot. Write each one as a short sentence, specific enough to check: “This customer gets files back in their own template.” “Refunds above 300 euros are approved by the finance lead.”.

    List every system you use and what each one is the source of truth for. You will find places where two systems describe the same thing differently. “Returned” in the ERP can mean the customer has sent the item back, while in the warehouse it means the item is back on the shelf.

    It has been revealed that the instinct is to make the systems agree. In my experience, that rarely works because each system was set up for the team that uses it, and that is why it works for them. Write the translation down instead. The same goes for numbers. In my company, the price did not sit in the same place from one customer to the next. Note where it lives for whom and which value to trust for which question.

    Recent findings suggest that most useful answers need two systems joined: the order in the web shop and the invoice in accounting, or the support ticket and the customer in the CRM. Find the field that ties them together and test it by hand. Take 20 random orders and look for them in the other system. If you find 19, you can build on that link. If you find 12, you cannot, and an agent will rarely tell you it is guessing. The test takes an afternoon and saves months of wrong reports.

    Industry observers note that split actions into four levels: read, propose, act after approval and act alone. Start with everything that changes something requiring approval from a named person. Set limits in money and volume, not in trust. When the agent has proposed the same action a hundred times without a mistake, move that one action up a level. That decision should be yours, never the agent’s.

    For every action, record who asked for it, who approved it, what happened and when. It sounds bureaucratic, but it is the only way to answer when a customer, an auditor or your board asks, “Why did this happen?” Without a log, you also cannot tell when it is safe to give the agent more freedom.

    According to recent reports, none of this is about artificial intelligence. It is about making knowledge that lives in people’s heads, and in systems that do not talk to each other, available and trustworthy. Companies that do this get more out of their AI. They also become less fragile when a key person goes on holiday or leaves.

    In a recent development, so start small. Book the two hours this week, write down 10 rules and test one link.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 20, 2026 at 1:00PM EST.
    • 10 stocks we like better than Intuitive Machines ›.
    • The commercial space race is expanding as private enterprises take over roles once reserved for governments.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 20, 2026 at 1:00PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Intuitive Machines ›.

    The commercial space race is expanding as private enterprises take over roles once reserved for governments. Investors weighing Intuitive Machines (LUNR -9.66%) against Rocket Lab (RKLB -8.96%) are looking for the best long-term winner.

    Both companies represent the growth of the modern space industry. Intuitive Machines focuses on lunar landing services and data infrastructure, while Rocket Lab provides reliable launch capabilities and satellite manufacturing.

    Industry observers note that intuitive Machines provides lunar spacecraft, communication networks, and infrastructure-as-a-service. It serves a mix of civil and national security clients, including NASA and the U.S. Space Development Agency. NASA accounted for roughly 78% of revenue in 2025, and customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

    In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $707 million, representing revenue growth of approximately 220.9%. The manufacturer reported a net loss of $128.0 million for the period. This resulted in a net margin of negative 18%.

    Recent findings suggest that as of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately negative 0.5x, indicating that total liabilities exceed shareholder equity. The current ratio of nearly 5.0x indicates the tech giant has sufficient short-term assets to cover its short-term debts. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was roughly negative $56 million, and many defense stocks are currently competing for similar infrastructure contracts.

    Industry observers note that rocket Lab is an end-to-end space provider that designs rockets and manufactures spacecraft components. It serves diverse markets including NASA, the National Reconnaissance Office, and various commercial satellite operators. Its top five customers accounted for nearly 49% of 2025 revenue, which requires careful monitoring by investors.

    It has been revealed that in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $881.9 million, about a 59% increase over the prior year. Rocket Lab reported a net loss of around $226.9 million during this time. These results produced a net margin of negative 25.7%.

    In a recent development, as of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.1x, which compares total debt to shareholder equity to show reliance on borrowing. The current ratio of nearly 4.1x shows strong short-term liquidity, even as free cash flow for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, was approximately negative $321.8 million. This cash consumption reflects the capital-intensive nature of building global launch infrastructure.

    Intuitive Machines faces significant customer concentration, as a vast majority of its revenue comes from NASA. The firm also deals with operational hazards inherent in space missions, including potential landing anomalies or mission failures. Additionally, the recent acquisition of Lanteris presents integration challenges and increased overhead costs.

    Industry observers note that rocket Lab must manage development risks associated with its latest Neutron launch vehicle, which recently suffered a tank failure during testing. The company is also exposed to operational hazards at its specific launch sites and relies heavily on key leadership. Finally, the pending acquisition of Iridium Communications (IRDM -2.68%) involves substantial financial risk and potential shareholder dilution.

    Intuitive Machines appears cheaper, carrying a lower Forward P/E relative to future earnings estimates and a lower P/S ratio based on sales over the past twelve months.

    Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

    Industry observers note that intuitive Machines has been posting superb results in fiscal 2026, most recently posting sequential quarterly growth of 31%, to $269 million in the third quarter reported in early November. Management says they have an order backlog of $1.9 billion, up $1.2 billion from the end of 2025. NASA is moving toward steady access-to-space flights and deliveries, too, which bodes well for the tech giant's longer-term sales. Revenue for fiscal 2026 is expected to more than quadruple to $935 million, though net loss is expected to widen to about $100 million. Analysts expect the business to turn a profit for the first time in 2029.

    According to recent reports, rocket Lab, meanwhile, made a huge splash in the market with its pending $8 billion acquisition of Iridium Communications this year. The combination promises to make Rocket Lab a space powerhouse by combining its launch technology with the communications spectrum offered by Iridium. In short, Rocket Lab could very well be a serious competitor to Space Exploration Technologies Corp (SPCX -6.19%). Don't overlook Rocket Lab's expertise in sending small payloads into orbit, and it is closing in on the same reusable rocket technology that SpaceX has used to lower its customer prices.

    Industry observers note that stand-alone Rocket Lab is seen boosting its revenue by more than 50% this year to $983 million, a figure analysts have raised throughout the year, with a net loss just about equal to 2025, at $199 million. The Iridium acquisition is a big meal to swallow, but the combined business should generate $1.8 billion in revenue in 2028, the first full year of the merged companies (The Iridium acquisition is slated to close mid-2027).

    Sources indicate that these are two exciting space-age stocks. Intuitive Machines, with its much more reasonable P/S and forward P/E ratios, gets the nod, under the adage of buying good companies at good prices for the long term, rather than paying extremely high premiums for future growth with Rocket Lab.
